acceptanceCriteria: Recognizably belongs to the Boars family and preserves every identity invariant.
Reads specifically as Razorback, T3, rather than another family form.
Communicates the Furrow-Cutting Specialist archetype and its battlefield duty.
Preserves coherent load-bearing anatomy, complete limbs, and believable ground contact.
Uses at least two normal construction dimensions without a palette-only or glow-only treatment.
Keeps the attack telegraph and counterplay signal visible at gameplay scale.
Frames one complete featured subject with no crop, labels, UI text, or watermark.
Output remains a candidate until independent approved-review evidence exists; it is never a runtime asset.
anatomyInvariants: Tall sail-like bristle ridge, asymmetric plow tusk, and visibly overbuilt shoulder on the cutting side.
Signature mechanic: Plow Curve: the inside tusk remains buried while the Razorback scores a visible curved path for its next charge.
battlefieldDuty: Cut a curved furrow whose route controls the next charge and throws debris outward.
constructionDimensions: Bristles, mud, hide, tusks, hooves, saliva, scars, and dust remain ordinary and materially distinct.
Charge weight reads through hoof trenches, shoulder compression, and displaced soil.
counterplay: Cross the furrow before launch or strike the rooted outside leg while the curve is being cut. Affinity signal: The pawing hoof, loaded hind legs, buried inside tusk, hooked obstacle, or scored stampede lane remains plainly visible.
forbiddenTreatments: Elemental glow or unexplained magical anatomy
Manufactured barding that hides the animal's shoulder and spine
identityInvariants: Every form keeps a low four-legged boar body, cloven hooves, mobile snout, raised bristles, short tail, and visible tusk roots.
Tier escalation uses tusk geometry, neck mass, shoulder callus, scars, and bristle profile rather than humanoid equipment.
Charge direction remains readable through hoof placement, lowered head angle, tusk contact, dust, and the alignment of the spine.
telegraph: The inside tusk stays in the soil and back bristles ripple along the future curve.
